creator_or_source: CRISP-DM: Consortium of NCR, DaimlerChrysler, SPSS (originally ISL), OHRA, and Teradata under EU ESPRIT funding. CRISP-ML(Q): Stefan Studer et al. at Mercedes-Benz AG Group Research and Machine Learning Group at Technische Universität Berlin
year_introduced: CRISP-DM: 1999 (conceived 1996, EU project 1997, published 1999-2000). CRISP-ML(Q): 2021 (arXiv preprint March 2020, published in Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction journal April 2021)
primary_url: CRISP-DM: https://www.datascience-pm.com/crisp-dm-2/ (best modern reference; original IBM/SPSS PDF at https://public.dhe.ibm.com/software/analytics/spss/documentation/modeler/14.2/es/CRISP-DM.pdf). CRISP-ML(Q): https://ml-ops.org/content/crisp-ml (practitioner guide) and https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.05155 (original paper)
scope: Full project lifecycle — from business understanding through deployment, plus monitoring and maintenance (CRISP-ML(Q))
key_components: CRISP-DM defines 6 phases in a cyclical, iterative process: (1) Business Understanding — define project objectives, business requirements, success criteria, and translate into data mining goals; (2) Data Understanding — collect initial data, explore and describe data, verify data quality, identify interesting subsets; (3) Data Preparation — select, clean, construct, integrate, and format data into the final dataset for modeling (typically 50-70% of project effort); (4) Modeling — select modeling techniques, generate test design, build model(s), assess model quality; (5) Evaluation — evaluate results against business objectives, review the process, determine next steps (deploy, iterate, or abandon); (6) Deployment — plan deployment, plan monitoring and maintenance, produce final report, review project. The phases are connected by arrows showing the most common iteration paths (e.g., Evaluation can loop back to Business Understanding). CRISP-ML(Q) extends this with three key modifications: (a) Business Understanding and Data Understanding are merged into a single phase because data availability directly constrains business feasibility — these cannot be assessed independently; (b) A 6th phase of Monitoring & Maintenance is added, with two sequential tasks: a Monitor task that evaluates model staleness and decides whether retraining is needed, and an Update task that retrains and re-evaluates the model; (c) A cross-cutting Quality Assurance (QA) methodology is applied at every phase, requiring for each task: definition of requirements and constraints (performance, data quality, robustness), specification of risks (bias, overfitting, lack of reproducibility, data leakage), and quality assurance methods to mitigate those risks (cross-validation, unit tests, documentation of process and results, statistical tests). The output documents of each phase are reviewed to rank risks and define next tasks, with re-iteration possible if quality criteria are not met.
typical_use_case: A data science team at a retail company wants to build a customer churn prediction model. Using CRISP-DM/CRISP-ML(Q): they start with Business Understanding (reduce churn by 10% in 6 months, define KPIs), merge with Data Understanding (explore purchase history, demographics, interaction logs, assess data completeness), proceed to Data Preparation (engineer features like average purchase frequency and days since last purchase, handle missing values), then Modeling (train gradient boosting and logistic regression, compare performance), Evaluation (validate against business success criteria — does targeting identified at-risk customers actually improve retention?), Deployment (integrate into CRM system for automated marketing triggers), and finally Monitoring & Maintenance (track prediction accuracy monthly, retrain quarterly as customer behavior shifts).
deliverables: CRISP-DM: project plan, data description report, data quality report, modeling report, evaluation report, deployment plan, final project report. CRISP-ML(Q) adds: scope document with success criteria, data quality verification report, feasibility assessment, risk register per phase, QA documentation, monitoring dashboard, and model update logs
genai_relevance: Medium. CRISP-DM's general structure (Business Understanding → Data → Modeling → Evaluation → Deployment) maps loosely to GenAI projects, but significant gaps exist. GenAI projects differ fundamentally in the Modeling phase (prompt engineering, RAG pipeline configuration, and fine-tuning replace traditional model training), the Data Preparation phase (curating prompt templates and evaluation datasets replaces tabular feature engineering), and require much heavier emphasis on guardrails, hallucination detection, and human feedback loops not covered by either framework. CRISP-ML(Q)'s quality assurance overlay and monitoring/maintenance phase are more relevant to LLMOps (monitoring drift, evaluating output quality), but neither framework was designed for the GenAI paradigm. A 2024 Medium article by Shreya Srinivas mapped the GenAI lifecycle to CRISP-DM, finding overlaps in scoping and evaluation but substantial differences in the modeling/adaptation phases. Practitioners increasingly combine CRISP-DM's structure with GenAI-specific lifecycle frameworks (LLMOps) for comprehensive coverage.
accessibility_for_non_engineers: High. CRISP-DM was designed to be industry- and tool-neutral, and its phase names (Business Understanding, Data Understanding, etc.) use accessible language. The framework does not require coding knowledge to understand or apply at a conceptual level. Business students can grasp the lifecycle and use it as a project management lens. The iterative nature and emphasis on Business Understanding as the starting point align well with entrepreneurial thinking. CRISP-ML(Q) is slightly more technical due to its QA methodology (discussing cross-validation, bias mitigation, statistical tests), but the high-level phases remain accessible.
time_to_apply: Multi-week to multi-month process for a real project. The framework guides an entire project lifecycle, not a single workshop. However, understanding the methodology and using it as a planning checklist takes 1-2 hours. A simplified classroom exercise (mapping an AI business idea to the 6 phases) can be done in a 30-60 minute workshop.
free_or_paid: Free. CRISP-DM 1.0 documentation is freely available (originally published by the consortium, now hosted by IBM). CRISP-ML(Q) paper is open access on arXiv and MDPI. The ml-ops.org practitioner guide is free. Templates available on GitHub (Jupyter notebook templates, cookie-cutter Python repos) and Notion Marketplace.
adoption_level: Industry standard. CRISP-DM is the most widely used data science/analytics methodology globally. KDnuggets polls (2002, 2004, 2007, 2014) consistently showed CRISP-DM as the #1 methodology, with 43% adoption in the 2014 poll. A 2009 review called it the 'de facto standard for developing data mining and knowledge discovery projects.' It remains the dominant framework in 2025 despite being 25+ years old and never officially updated past version 1.0. CRISP-ML(Q) is emerging as the modern ML-specific extension, gaining traction in MLOps communities, cited 400+ times since 2021, and referenced by organizations like Mercedes-Benz and Cisco.
ai_project_stage: Multiple — covers Ideation (Business Understanding), PoC (Data Understanding + Modeling), MVP (Evaluation), Production (Deployment), and Maintenance (Monitoring & Maintenance in CRISP-ML(Q))
relevance_for_entrepreneurs: Essential foundational knowledge. CRISP-DM teaches entrepreneurs that AI projects are not linear — the iterative cycle between Business Understanding, Data, and Modeling prevents the common startup mistake of building models before understanding data constraints. The emphasis on Business Understanding as Phase 1 forces entrepreneurs to define success criteria and ROI expectations before investing in data infrastructure. For pitching to investors or enterprise clients, speaking the CRISP-DM language signals project maturity. CRISP-ML(Q)'s quality assurance overlay helps entrepreneurs anticipate production risks (model degradation, data drift, bias) that kill AI products post-launch. Understanding these frameworks also helps entrepreneurs evaluate AI vendors and consultants — if a vendor skips Business Understanding or has no monitoring plan, that is a red flag.
session_mapping: S3 (Projects) — primary session for AI project framing and management. Also relevant to S1 (Fundamentals) for introducing how AI projects work, and S5 (Ethics/Governance) for the quality assurance and risk mitigation aspects of CRISP-ML(Q).
complements: AI Project Canvas and Machine Learning Canvas (Louis Dorard) — these canvases serve as structured tools for the Business Understanding phase of CRISP-DM, translating business requirements into ML specifications on a single page. Andrew Ng's AI Transformation Playbook — provides the organizational change management layer that CRISP-DM lacks (team building, training, strategy). Build vs Buy vs Fine-tune vs RAG Decision Matrix — helps with the key decision point during Business Understanding about whether to build custom AI at all. NIST AI Risk Management Framework — provides the governance framework that maps to CRISP-ML(Q)'s quality assurance methodology. Data-Centric AI Methodology (Andrew Ng) — complements the Data Preparation phase with a modern philosophy of systematically improving data quality rather than tweaking models.
limitations: 1) CRISP-DM has not been updated since 1999 — it predates big data, cloud computing, deep learning, and GenAI, making some tasks feel dated. 2) The Deployment phase is chronically underspecified — most implementations skip it entirely, and CRISP-DM provides little guidance on MLOps, CI/CD, or production monitoring. 3) Not a true project management methodology — assumes a single person or small team, ignoring stakeholder communication, team coordination, sprint planning, and resource allocation. 4) No agile integration — the phase-based structure can feel waterfall-like, though the framework officially supports iteration. Researchers have proposed 'Agile CRISP-DM' variants. 5) CRISP-ML(Q) addresses some gaps but remains focused on classical ML — it does not cover GenAI-specific concerns (prompt engineering, hallucination, RAG evaluation, RLHF). 6) Neither framework addresses ethical considerations, fairness, or regulatory compliance explicitly (EU AI Act, GDPR), requiring supplementary frameworks like ALTAI or NIST AI RMF. 7) The KDnuggets adoption polls are self-selected and date from 2014 — actual current adoption rates are uncertain, though CRISP-DM remains the most commonly referenced methodology in data science education.
example_application: A French e-commerce startup wants to implement AI-powered product recommendations to increase average order value. Using CRISP-DM/CRISP-ML(Q): Phase 1 (Business & Data Understanding) — the team defines the goal as increasing AOV by 15% within 6 months, identifies available data (purchase history of 50K users, product catalog, browsing sessions), and assesses feasibility (sufficient transaction volume for collaborative filtering, GDPR compliance for user data). Phase 2 (Data Preparation) — they clean purchase logs, create user-item interaction matrices, engineer features like recency, frequency, and monetary value per user. Phase 3 (Modeling) — they train collaborative filtering and content-based models, compare against a simple popularity baseline. Phase 4 (Evaluation) — they run an A/B test measuring actual AOV uplift vs. the current rule-based system. Phase 5 (Deployment) — the winning model is deployed via API into the checkout flow, with the team documenting the deployment plan. Phase 6 (Monitoring & Maintenance) — they track recommendation click-through rates and AOV weekly, set up alerts for model staleness, and plan quarterly retraining as the product catalog and user base evolve. QA throughout: document data quality checks, validate for popularity bias in recommendations, test model robustness to cold-start users.
available_templates: CRISP-DM: Notion template on Notion Marketplace (Data Science Project CRISP-DM Approach), GitHub repositories (RyusukeKimura/crisp-dm, MichaelVerdegaal/crisp-dm-template), Jupyter notebook template (patiegm/Datasci_Resources), PowerPoint/Canva templates on SlideEgg, Creately online diagram editor. CRISP-ML(Q): the ml-ops.org website provides a comprehensive practitioner reference with phase-by-phase guidance, and the original paper (arXiv:2003.05155) includes process diagrams and QA flowcharts that can serve as templates. Udemy course available for structured learning.
regulatory_alignment: Indirect alignment only. Neither CRISP-DM nor CRISP-ML(Q) was designed for regulatory compliance. However, CRISP-ML(Q)'s quality assurance methodology (risk identification, documentation requirements, bias detection, reproducibility) creates natural touchpoints with EU AI Act requirements (risk assessment, technical documentation, human oversight) and GDPR principles (data quality, purpose limitation). The monitoring and maintenance phase aligns with EU AI Act Article 9 (risk management system) requirements for continuous monitoring of high-risk AI systems. For formal compliance, CRISP-DM/CRISP-ML(Q) should be supplemented with dedicated regulatory frameworks like NIST AI RMF or ISO 42001.
